blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The z-test compares a sample statistic with a hypothesised value by asking how many standard errors apart they are, and reads the p-value from the standard Normal distribution. For a mean with known population SD σ,

z = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (σ ÷ √n).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: This is a z-score (recall §5.7.2.2.1) computed for a sample statistic instead of a single child’s value. Under H₀ the sample mean is centred on μ₀ with SD σ/√n (recall §6.7), and by the Central Limit Theorem (§6.6) its sampling distribution is close to Normal. So z behaves like a standard Normal variable when H₀ is true, and a large |z| is evidence against H₀.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A district’s sample of 100 newborns has mean birthweight 2.9 kg. Test it against a hypothesised reference value of 3.0 kg, assuming σ = 0.5 kg is known from a large earlier survey.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. SE = 0.5 ÷ √100 = 0.05 kg.
  2. z = (2.9 − 3.0) ÷ 0.05 = −2.00.
  3. Two-sided p = 2 × P(Z < −2.00) = 2 × 0.0228 = 0.046.
  4. At α = 0.05, reject H₀: a mean 2 SEs below 3.0 kg would be unusual if the true mean were 3.0 kg (recall the steps of §8.7).

points.html: The general form is z = (statistic − hypothesised value) ÷ SE. It needs either a known σ (rare) or a sample large enough that the Normal approximation holds. “n ≥ 30” is a convention, not a law: strongly skewed data need more (recall §6.6).
When σ is estimated by s, use the t-test (§9.2.1) at any sample size (recall §5.7.2.3).
For proportions σ is not a separate unknown: under H₀ it is fixed by p₀. That is why the z-test remains a standard large-sample test for proportions (§9.1.1–§9.1.2).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The one-proportion z-test compares an observed proportion p̂ = x/n with a hypothesised proportion p₀:

z = (p̂ − p₀) ÷ √[p₀(1 − p₀) ÷ n].

When n is small, the exact binomial test replaces it and computes the p-value directly from the Binomial(n, p₀) distribution.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Each person contributes a 0/1 outcome, a Bernoulli variable with variance p(1 − p) (recall §5.7.1.1). The proportion p̂ is the mean of these 0s and 1s, so its SE is √[p(1 − p)/n] (recall §6.7). The test assumes H₀ is true, so it puts p₀, not p̂, into the SE. (The confidence interval of §7.2.2 uses p̂, because it makes no assumption about the true value.) The Normal approximation is adequate when np₀ and n(1 − p₀) are both at least 5, a common convention (recall §5.7.2.2.4). Below that, count the binomial probabilities exactly.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Recall the infant cohort of §8.7 (200 infants followed up at two PHCs; the same data return in §10.6.3, §10.6.4 and §11.7): 120 were exclusively breastfed (EBF). The district’s planning target, used here as a hypothetical H₀, is 70%.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. p̂ = 120/200 = 0.60. Check: np₀ = 140 and n(1 − p₀) = 60, both ≥ 5.
  2. SE under H₀ = √(0.70 × 0.30 ÷ 200) = √0.00105 = 0.0324.
  3. z = (0.60 − 0.70) ÷ 0.0324 = −3.09; two-sided p = 0.002. EBF coverage is below the target.

Small sample: one anganwadi. In one anganwadi, 7 of 15 infants were exclusively breastfed. Test against p₀ = 0.70.

  1. Check: np₀ = 10.5 but n(1 − p₀) = 4.5 < 5. The Normal approximation is doubtful.
  2. The exact test uses Binomial(15, 0.70). P(X = 7) = 0.0348. The two-sided exact p-value adds the probabilities of every outcome no more likely than the one observed: P(X ≤ 7) = 0.0500, plus P(X = 14) = 0.0305 and P(X = 15) = 0.0047, which gives p = 0.085.
  3. The z approximation gives z = (0.467 − 0.70) ÷ √(0.21/15) = −1.97 and p = 0.049. It would call the result “significant”; the exact test does not. With small n, trust the exact test.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
eb <- read.csv("data/ebf_diarrhoea_cohort.csv")
x <- sum(eb$not_ebf == 0); n <- nrow(eb); c(x = x, n = n)
prop.test(x, n, p = 0.70, correct = FALSE)
binom.test(7, 15, p = 0.70)
  x   n 
120 200 

    1-sample proportions test without continuity correction
X-squared = 9.5238, df = 1, p-value = 0.002028
...
    Exact binomial test
number of successes = 7, number of trials = 15, p-value = 0.08528
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2126667 0.7341387

prop.test reports X-squared = 9.52, which is z² = (−3.086)²; its p-value, 0.002, is the z-test’s. binom.test gives the exact p = 0.085 for the anganwadi and an exact 95% CI (recall §7.2.4) of 21% to 73%, which includes the 70% target.

points.html: SE in the test uses p₀; SE in the CI uses p̂. With p̂ far from p₀ the two differ.

Check np₀ and n(1 − p₀) before trusting z. The exact binomial test is widely available in statistical software and is the usual choice for small n; the sign test (§10.1.1) is this same test applied to the signs of paired differences.
A survey that sampled villages rather than individuals needs an SE that allows for clustering (recall DEFF, §6.2.6); the formula above assumes independent individuals.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The two-proportion z-test compares proportions p̂₁ = x₁/n₁ and p̂₂ = x₂/n₂ from two independent groups:

z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂) ÷ √[p̄(1 − p̄)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)], where p̄ = (x₁ + x₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂)

is the pooled proportion. For a 2×2 table, z² equals the Pearson chi-square statistic, so the two-sided z-test and the chi-square test of independence (§10.6.1, which compares observed and expected counts in each cell) are the same test.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: H₀ says both groups share one true proportion. The best estimate of that common value pools both groups, p̄, and the SE under H₀ uses it. The confidence interval for the difference makes no such assumption, so it uses the separate, unpooled SE of §7.2.3. The same pattern as §9.1.1 holds: test under H₀, estimate without it.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
SE. Variances of independent estimates add (recall §7.2.3): Var(p̂₁ − p̂₂) = p₁(1 − p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1 − p₂)/n₂. Under H₀, p₁ = p₂ = p, so this becomes p(1 − p)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂), estimated with p̄.

z² = χ². Write N = n₁ + n₂, and m₁, m₂ for the column totals (with and without the outcome). The expected count for a cell is row total × column total ÷ N. For the top-left cell, O − E = x₁ − n₁m₁/N = n₁n₂(p̂₁ − p̂₂)/N, and every cell has the same |O − E|. Then

χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = (O − E)² × N³/(n₁n₂m₁m₂) = N n₁n₂(p̂₁ − p̂₂)² ÷ (m₁m₂),

since Σ1/E = N(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)(1/m₁ + 1/m₂). Put p̄ = m₁/N and 1 − p̄ = m₂/N into z²: its denominator p̄(1 − p̄)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂) = m₁m₂/(N n₁n₂), which gives the same expression. So z² = χ² with 1 degree of freedom, as z² = χ²₁ requires (recall §5.7.2.5).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
The same 200-infant cohort, by feeding and diarrhoea during follow-up:

Diarrhoea No diarrhoea Total
Not EBF 33 47 80
EBF 14 106 120
Total 47 153 200

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
eb <- read.csv("data/ebf_diarrhoea_cohort.csv")
tab <- table(not_ebf = factor(eb$not_ebf, levels = c(1, 0)),
             diarrhoea = factor(eb$diarrhoea, levels = c(1, 0)))
tab
prop.test(tab, correct = FALSE)
       diarrhoea
not_ebf   1   0
      1  33  47
      0  14 106

    2-sample test for equality of proportions without continuity
    correction
X-squared = 23.367, df = 1, p-value = 1.338e-06
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1736206 0.4180461
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.4125000 0.1166667

The table reproduces the counts. X-squared = 23.367 is z² (step 5), and the p-value matches step 3. The CI (0.174 to 0.418) is the unpooled interval of step 4. R reports the test as a chi-square; it is the same test as the z-test.

points.html: Pooled SE for the test, unpooled SE for the CI. The z-test and the uncorrected 2×2 chi-square give identical two-sided p-values; only z can be one-sided.
The difference, 29.6 percentage points, is the risk difference. The risk ratio and odds ratio for the same table come in §10.6.4.

This is an association in an observational cohort, not an effect of breastfeeding: mothers who breastfeed exclusively may differ in other ways, including which PHC they attend. §11.7 (stratified analysis) shows that PHC explains part of the association.
With small expected counts use Fisher’s exact test (§10.7, which computes exact probabilities for the 2×2 table).

questions.prompt: In a block, 45 of 60 sampled children are fully immunised. Test against a target of 85%. Check the Normal-approximation condition first, then give z and the two-sided p-value.
questions.answer: Condition: np₀ = 60 × 0.85 = 51 and n(1 − p₀) = 60 × 0.15 = 9, both ≥ 5, so the Normal approximation is acceptable (a convention, §5.7.2.2.4). p̂ = 45/60 = 0.75. SE under H₀ = √(0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 60) = √0.002125 = 0.0461. z = (0.75 − 0.85) ÷ 0.0461 = −2.17. Two-sided p = 2 × P(Z < −2.17) = 0.030. At α = 0.05, coverage is below the 85% target. If the 60 children came from a few villages, the SE should allow for clustering (§6.2.6).

questions.prompt: ORS use during the last diarrhoea episode was 60/100 in Block A and 45/100 in Block B. Compute the two-proportion z statistic, then the Pearson χ² from the expected counts, and show that χ² = z².
Why does the one-proportion test use p₀ in the SE while the confidence interval uses p̂?
questions.answer: A test calculates how surprising the data would be if H₀ were true, so every part of the calculation, including the SE, assumes p = p₀. A confidence interval makes no assumption about the true value; it estimates the SE from the data, using p̂.
